notes: Tuesday 10 Nov 2026 world issue (Taipei ~08:00). Window: Mon 9 Nov. Economy: Boeing cuts 5%; PepsiCo 1,000 jobs; UK low-wind power call; Children's Place bankruptcy. Tech (USA): FBI probes Huang affair; Anthropic Fable/Mythos 5.2; CoreWeave doom-cycle; Senate permitting bill, data centers pay. Politics: Massie impeachment of Hegseth; Trump doubts midterms; Pope Leo rebukes Milei; Trump says Iran war over. Literature (USA): Biden memoir tour cut NOT; Fisketjon dies NOT; Hoffman memoir HOT; Capote auction HOT. Social: Senegal migrant boat; Russell Brand sentenced; Gaza landslide; Queensland rape-case report.

stories.headline: Boeing will cut about 5% of its passenger-jet workers because building planes is going slower than planned
stories.dek: Layoff notices start in December; Boeing now hopes to reach 52 of its 737 Max jets a month in late 2027.
stories.caveman: Boeing is one of the world's two big makers of passenger planes. It planned to build more 737 Max jets each month, but making the wings has gone slower than expected. Fewer planes means Boeing has more workers than it needs. So the head of its commercial-plane unit, Stephanie Pope, told staff it will cut about 5% of that workforce. Some will happen by not replacing people who leave; the rest are layoffs, with notices starting in December. Boeing is trying to hold steady at about 47 Max jets a month and hopes to hit 52 a month in the second half of 2027.
stories.why_it_matters: Airlines around the world, including in Asia, are waiting for new planes. Slow deliveries can mean fewer flights and higher ticket prices. And thousands of factory families feel the job cuts.
stories.camps: Boeing says it must match staff to a slower plan. Unions and workers say workers keep paying for management mistakes. Safety advocates say going slow is better than rushing after Boeing's past quality problems.
stories.image_alt: Boeing 737 Max jets on the factory floor

terms.explain: When a company tells workers their jobs are ending.
Shrinking staff by not replacing people who quit or retire.
Boeing's best-selling single-aisle passenger plane.
How many planes a factory finishes each month.

stories.headline: PepsiCo cuts about 1,000 jobs as Americans buy fewer of its drinks and snacks
stories.dek: North American drink sales fell 2% last quarter even after price cuts and more ads.
stories.caveman: PepsiCo makes Pepsi, Gatorade, Lay's chips and Doritos. Its home business in North America is struggling: in the last three months, it sold 2% fewer drinks, and snack sales were flat. The company already cut prices and spent more on ads, but the fix is taking longer than hoped. Now it will cut about 1,000 jobs over the next week, saying it wants to be faster and better connected. PepsiCo has about 306,000 workers worldwide, about 125,000 in the US. Its stock is down almost 1% this year while the overall US market is up about 11%.
stories.why_it_matters: Big food companies are a sign of how ordinary shoppers feel. When people buy fewer chips and sodas, it often means budgets are tight — or tastes are moving to healthier choices and weight-loss drugs.
stories.camps: The company says it is making the business stronger. Workers say job cuts are an easy fix for bosses. Some health experts note people may simply be drinking less sugar, which is not bad news for everyone.
stories.image_alt: Bottles of Pepsi

terms.explain: How many items a company sold, not how much money it made.
A company's guess of how much profit it will make.
An index of 500 big US companies, used to measure the US stock market.

stories.headline: Britain's power operator makes a rare morning call for more electricity as the wind stops blowing across Europe
stories.dek: The shortfall shrank and was cancelled by 9am — officials say there was never a risk of blackouts.
stories.caveman: Great Britain gets a lot of its electricity from wind. On Monday, forecasts showed very little wind across Europe. The National Energy System Operator (Neso), which keeps supply and demand balanced every minute, warned on Sunday night that it was about 1,400 megawatts short for Monday morning — and asked power plants to offer about 800 more, like one medium gas plant. Power companies stepped up. The gap shrank to 500, then 200, and the warning was cancelled just after 9am. Such notices used to come mostly on cold winter evenings; now they are showing up at odd times, even in summer heatwaves.
stories.why_it_matters: As countries switch to wind and solar, they need backup for calm, dark days — batteries, gas plants, or power cables to neighbors. Taiwan faces the same puzzle as it grows renewable energy.
stories.camps: Neso says this was routine and safe. Clean-energy supporters say it shows why more storage and grid links are needed. Critics of fast green policy say it proves the system still depends on gas.
stories.image_alt: Offshore wind turbines

terms.explain: A unit of electric power. 1 megawatt can run hundreds of homes.
A warning that the spare power cushion is getting thin.
The network of power plants and wires that carries electricity.

stories.headline: Children's Place, a big US kids' clothing chain, files for bankruptcy and looks for a buyer
stories.dek: Its 514 stores stay open for now; the company blames tariffs and slower shopping.
stories.caveman: The Children's Place sells clothes for babies and kids, and also owns Gymboree. It has 514 stores in North America and sells in 13 countries. On Sunday it filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy, which lets a company keep running while it deals with debts. It wants offers from buyers by December 9 and hopes to close a sale by the end of December. Stores and websites stay open for now. The company says tariffs (taxes on imported goods) and shoppers spending less hurt it. A Saudi investment firm, Mithaq Capital, took control in 2024 when it was already in trouble, but things did not turn around.
stories.why_it_matters: Most kids' clothes are made in Asia. Tariffs raise their cost, and families feel it. A big chain closing can also mean lost jobs at malls.
stories.camps: Free-trade supporters say tariffs are pushing stores like this over the edge. Tariff supporters say retailers relied too much on cheap imports. Others say the bigger problem is shoppers moving online to cheaper sites.
stories.image_alt: A Children's Place store front

terms.explain: A type of US bankruptcy that lets a company keep operating while it fixes its debts or sells itself.
Taxes a country puts on goods coming in from other countries.
Things a company owns that have value — stores, brands, stock.

stories.headline: Trump says the FBI is investigating Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy
stories.dek: Nvidia lost about $250 billion in value on Monday as shares fell about 4%.
stories.caveman: Jensen Huang runs Nvidia, the company that makes most of the chips powering AI. On Sunday he admitted he had an affair. US intelligence officials believe the woman, Alice Huang (no relation), who ran Singapore company Megaspeed, was a spy for China, the New York Times reported. President Trump said Monday the FBI is now looking into it. He said he called Huang, who told him he had no idea she was a spy — and Trump said he believes him. Nvidia's board started its own independent investigation and says it sees no sign that secrets leaked. China calls the claims groundless. Lawmakers from several committees want Huang at a closed-door briefing next week.
stories.why_it_matters: Nvidia is the most important company in the AI boom and a huge customer for Taiwan chipmakers. Any risk that its secrets or chips reached China is a national-security question for the US — and a market worry for Taiwan.
stories.camps: Trump and many tech leaders are standing by Huang. Democrats and some Republicans want answers on what officials knew and when. Some reporting says US officials were warned last spring. China says it is a smear.
stories.image_alt: Donald Trump and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang

terms.explain: The US federal police agency that also hunts spies.
Spying — secretly gathering information for another government.
A probe run by outside lawyers, not the company's own bosses.
A private meeting with lawmakers, not open to the public.

stories.headline: Anthropic releases faster, cheaper Claude models — its first big launch since its CEO called for slowing AI down
stories.dek: Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 arrive as the company prepares a stock-market debut that could value it at $1–1.5 trillion.
stories.caveman: Anthropic is a US AI company that makes the Claude chatbot. On Monday it released two new top models, Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2. It says they answer 30% faster and cost 20% less than the last version. In September its CEO, Dario Amodei, had called for slowing the pace of AI. The company says this is "pacing, not pausing" and that the models went through extra safety tests. Mythos is powerful at cybersecurity, so access has been limited; Fable is a public version with more guardrails. Anthropic is getting ready to sell shares to the public, possibly as soon as next week, aiming for a value of $1 trillion to $1.5 trillion.
stories.why_it_matters: This tests whether a company that talks a lot about AI safety can also win in a cut-throat market. The IPO is also a big signal for whether investors still believe in AI after recent stock crashes.
stories.camps: Supporters say careful releases with new safety checks are the responsible path. Critics say "slow down" means little if new models keep coming. Investors worry about high costs and growing anti-AI anger in US politics.
stories.image_alt: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei at the company's San Francisco headquarters

terms.explain: The most advanced AI systems at the cutting edge.
Initial public offering — when a company first sells shares on the stock market.
Small pieces of text AI reads and writes; AI is often priced per million tokens.
Safety limits built into an AI to stop harmful uses.

stories.headline: AI cloud renter CoreWeave faces a 'doom cycle' fear: lenders get nervous as voters turn against data centers
stories.dek: Its bonds now pay over 16%, a sign lenders see real risk; results come out Tuesday.
stories.caveman: CoreWeave is a "neocloud": a company that buys huge numbers of Nvidia chips and rents that computing power to AI firms. It pays for the chips mostly with borrowed money. In the past month, neocloud stock prices fell by half. In last week's US elections, voters rejected data centers in 40 of 41 local ballot measures, and Democrats won many governor races. Lenders now worry. Some CoreWeave bonds pay above 16% interest, and the cost of insurance against it failing to repay jumped 50% in a month. The "doom cycle" fear: tighter loans slow building, which hurts income, which makes loans even harder. CoreWeave's CEO says customer deals are not affected.
stories.why_it_matters: A lot of the AI boom runs on debt. If lenders pull back, AI building slows — which would affect Taiwan's server and chip makers.
stories.camps: Bulls say demand for AI computing is still huge and the panic is overdone. Bears say too much borrowing on hopeful growth looks like past bubbles. Local residents who voted no say they are protecting their power bills, water and land.
stories.image_alt: CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator on CNBC at the New York Stock Exchange

terms.explain: A newer company that rents out AI computing power, competing with Amazon, Microsoft and Google.
The interest a borrower must pay; higher means lenders see more risk.
Insurance investors buy in case a company can't repay its debt.
A giant building full of computers that power the internet and AI.

stories.headline: US Senate moves forward a bill to build power plants and power lines faster — and make AI data centers pay for their own electricity
stories.dek: The 73–25 vote opens debate; Trump and many Democrats both back it.
stories.caveman: In the US, big projects like power plants, mines and power lines can wait years for environmental reviews. A bipartisan bill (supported by both parties), the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, would speed up those reviews by changing several environmental laws. It would also make it easier to approve new power lines. And it would force AI companies and data-center builders to pay for the power and grid upgrades they need, instead of everyday customers. On Monday the Senate voted 73–25 to start debate. Republicans want to build faster in general; Democrats want faster solar and wind. Backers want it passed before the current Congress ends in January.
stories.why_it_matters: Data centers are driving up power demand and, in some places, household bills. Who pays for new power is becoming a big political fight.
stories.camps: Supporters say the US cannot build clean energy or anything else under today's slow rules. Environmental groups worry faster reviews mean less protection for nature and local communities. Some say making AI firms pay is a fair, overdue change.
stories.image_alt: High-voltage electricity power lines

terms.explain: Getting government approval to build something.
Supported by both major US parties.
The weeks after an election when the old Congress is still in charge.
Big power lines that carry electricity long distances.

stories.headline: A Republican congressman forces a House vote on impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth
stories.dek: Thomas Massie lists eight charges; Trump says "I'll stand by him."
stories.caveman: Impeachment is how the US Congress can charge a top official with serious wrongdoing — like a work firing, not a prison sentence. Rep. Thomas Massie, a Republican from Kentucky, filed articles of impeachment against Pete Hegseth, who runs the military, with eight charges of "high crimes and misdemeanors." That sets up a House vote within about two days. Massie lost his primary this year after Hegseth campaigned for his opponent. He says the core issue is whether Congress really controls decisions to go to war. Hegseth calls it a "sham." Trump backs him: "He won two wars."
stories.why_it_matters: It is rare for a president's own party to push to impeach his cabinet member. It also tests Congress's power over war, after the long US war with Iran.
stories.camps: Massie and critics say Hegseth must answer for how wars were run. Hegseth and Trump call it revenge by a defeated lawmaker. Some Democrats, who take power in January, say tougher oversight is coming anyway.
stories.image_alt: Rep. Thomas Massie at the US Capitol
stories.image_credit: Photo: Roberto Schmidt / Getty Images via NPR

terms.explain: When the House formally charges an official with wrongdoing; the Senate then decides whether to remove them.
The Constitution's phrase for serious abuse of power.
The rules on who can send the US into war — Congress or the president.
An election inside a party to pick its candidate.

stories.headline: Trump questions whether the midterm elections were honest — days after saying he would accept the results
stories.dek: He offered no evidence; experts and officials say the vote went smoothly.
stories.caveman: Last week, Democrats won control of both the House and the Senate. On election night Trump told the New York Times he was "absolutely willing" to accept the results. On Monday he posted on Truth Social: "Does anybody really believe that this 'Election' was honest?" He made vague claims about polls, vote "dumps" and "machines" without specific proof. State and local officials said voting was mostly problem-free. An MIT election expert said vote counts came in with the normal, expected patterns. A few races, including Senate seats in Alaska and Mississippi, are still not called.
stories.why_it_matters: When a leader doubts elections without proof, people may lose trust in voting itself — even people on the winning side. That can make peaceful handovers of power harder.
stories.camps: Trump's supporters say they are just asking questions about surprise results. Election officials of both parties say the system worked. Democracy experts warn that repeated fraud claims without evidence wear down faith in democracy.
stories.image_alt: Donald Trump speaking

terms.explain: US elections held halfway through a president's four-year term.
Whether a result is accepted as fair and real.
Illegal voting; studies show it is extremely rare in the US.
When media declare a race winner after enough votes are counted.

stories.headline: Pope Leo tells Argentina's President Milei: the economy must serve people, not the other way round
stories.dek: On his first stop in the late Pope Francis's home country, Leo defends the poor, pensioners and disabled people hit by cuts.
stories.caveman: Javier Milei, Argentina's president, has made deep spending cuts (called austerity) for three years to fight inflation — including cuts to help for disabled people. Pope Leo XIV, head of the world's 1.4 billion Catholics, arrived in Buenos Aires on Sunday. Standing with Milei, he said "the economy must be at the service of the people." He spoke up for poor families, pensioners and the sick. He also hinted at Milei's harsh language, saying democracy needs listening and careful words. Huge crowds cheered. It is the first papal visit to Argentina in nearly 40 years, and Leo is touring just three weeks after lung-cancer surgery.
stories.why_it_matters: Argentina is a big test of whether harsh cuts can fix a broken economy. The pope's words give weight to people who say the poor are paying the price.
stories.camps: Milei's supporters say austerity brought inflation down and saved the economy. Critics, unions and many Catholics say it hurt the weakest. Some say the pope should stay out of politics; others say defending the poor is his job.
stories.image_alt: Pope Leo shakes hands with Argentine president Javier Milei in Buenos Aires
stories.image_credit: Photo: Daniel Dal Zennaro / EPA via The Guardian

terms.explain: Big government spending cuts to reduce debt or inflation.
When prices rise quickly and money buys less.
Another word for the pope.

stories.headline: Trump says the US war with Iran is 'effectively over' and new attacks don't seem necessary
stories.dek: Gulf leaders lobbied him not to restart fighting; the US naval blockade stays for now.
stories.caveman: The US and Iran have been at war for almost nine months. Before the US midterm elections, the US kept sending troops to the Middle East, and some expected new strikes afterward. On Monday, after meeting Qatar's prime minister, Trump said more military action "doesn't seem to be a very necessary thing" and that the war is "effectively over" — but the US is "locked and loaded" if needed. He said Gulf states prefer the current situation: a huge US naval blockade. Trump has claimed a peace deal was close many times before. Vice-President JD Vance said the war was a key reason Republicans lost the midterms.
stories.why_it_matters: The war has pushed up oil prices worldwide, including in Taiwan. Calmer talk already helped oil fall to its lowest level since August.
stories.camps: Supporters say pressure worked and the blockade keeps Iran in check. Critics say Trump often overstates progress and the war has no clear plan. Gulf neighbors mainly want to avoid more missiles flying.
stories.image_alt: Donald Trump speaks to reporters in the White House briefing room
stories.image_credit: Photo: Alex Brandon / AP via The Guardian

terms.explain: Using ships to stop goods going in or out of a country.
Making a conflict bigger or more violent.
Arab countries along the Persian Gulf, like Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the UAE.

stories.headline: NOT so hot: Joe Biden cuts back his book tour as his cancer advances — but his memoir 'Promise Me America' still lands Nov. 17
stories.dek: The former president says some days are better than others; the book calls Jan. 6 a shame that should follow Trump "to his grave."
stories.caveman: Joe Biden was US president from 2021 to 2025. In May 2025 he was diagnosed with an aggressive prostate cancer. His White House memoir, Promise Me America, comes out on November 17. Usually a big memoir means a long tour of interviews and events. But Biden posted that his illness "slows me down," so he will do far fewer talks and hopes "the words on the page speak for themselves." Much of the book covers the January 6, 2021 attack on the US Capitol by Trump supporters. Biden writes plainly that "Donald Trump led an insurrection."
stories.why_it_matters: Presidential memoirs are major publishing events and part of how history gets written. Fewer appearances may hurt sales — and fewer chances to answer questions about his age and record.
stories.camps: Fans see a moving, last-word book from a man facing illness. Critics, including some Democrats, still blame Biden for staying in the 2024 race too long. Trump supporters reject his account of January 6.
stories.image_alt: Joe Biden speaks to a crowd in Columbia, South Carolina
stories.image_credit: Photo: Sean Rayford / Getty Images via The Guardian

terms.explain: A book where someone tells the story of their own life.
Events and interviews an author does to promote a new book.
A violent uprising against the government.

stories.headline: NOT: Gary Fisketjon, the editor behind Cormac McCarthy, Donna Tartt and Don DeLillo, dies at 72
stories.dek: He launched Vintage Contemporaries in 1984 and spent 29 years at Knopf shaping modern American fiction.
stories.caveman: Book editors work behind the scenes: they pick books and help writers make them better. Gary Fisketjon was one of the most famous. In 1984 he started Vintage Contemporaries, a paperback line that made young writers cool to read. At Knopf, for 29 years, he worked with Cormac McCarthy, Donna Tartt, Don DeLillo, Jay McInerney, Joy Williams, Tobias Wolff and others — many now seen as classics of late-20th-century American fiction. He was known for very close, line-by-line editing. Knopf let him go in 2019 for breaking company policy; in 2025 he started a new fiction imprint, Panamerica. Knopf's publisher called him "the foremost literary editor of his generation."
stories.why_it_matters: Many books we call "great American novels" passed through an editor's hands. His death marks the end of an era of star editors.
stories.camps: Writers and publishers praise his eye and care. His 2019 exit is a reminder that his career also had a messy end; the reason was not made public.
stories.image_alt: Editor Gary Fisketjon

terms.explain: The person at a publisher who chooses books and helps writers improve them.
A brand name a publisher uses for a line of books.
A famous New York book publisher.

stories.headline: HOT: Dustin Hoffman's memoir 'Look at Me' — the star of The Graduate finally tells his side
stories.dek: Ghostwritten with New Yorker writer Ariel Levy, it sets the record straight on the famous "Try acting, dear boy" story.
stories.caveman: Dustin Hoffman is an American actor famous for The Graduate, Rain Man and Tootsie. His new autobiography is called Look at Me. The title comes from British actor Laurence Olivier, who once told him acting is really about saying "look at me." A Guardian review says the book was written with help from New Yorker writer Ariel Levy. One big reveal: the legend that Hoffman stayed up all night to look tired "for his art," and Olivier mocked him, is wrong. Hoffman says he was really out partying, and a magazine writer twisted the story to make him look silly.
stories.why_it_matters: Celebrity memoirs are some of the biggest sellers in US publishing, especially near the holidays. This one is getting serious reviews, not just gossip coverage.
stories.camps: Fans enjoy the inside stories about classic films. Some readers want more honesty about past accusations of sexual misconduct against Hoffman, which he has apologized for. Critics debate whether ghostwritten memoirs are really the star's own voice.
stories.image_alt: Dustin Hoffman in The Graduate
stories.image_credit: Photo: Bettmann Archive via The Guardian

terms.explain: A life story written by (or with) the person themselves.
A writer who helps write a book published under someone else's name.
An acting style where actors try to really live the feelings of a role.

stories.headline: HOT (and weird): Truman Capote's belongings go up for auction — including his dog's ashes
stories.dek: "The Magpie and the Swans" sale lists items from his New York apartment and Long Island house.
stories.caveman: Truman Capote was a famous American writer of Breakfast at Tiffany's and In Cold Blood. He died in 1984. His biographer and friend Gerald Clarke has looked after his things for 40 years. Now they are being sold in a public auction called "The Magpie and the Swans." A magpie is a bird known for collecting shiny things — like Capote, who loved glitter and comfort. Lit Hub picked nine of the strangest items: a bulldog tote bag, decorative dog heads, a leopard-head ashtray, solid gold safety pins, early Richard Avedon photos — and the ashes of his beloved bulldog.
stories.why_it_matters: Writers' homes and objects help fans feel close to them, and auctions like this keep a writer's fame alive for new generations.
stories.camps: Fans and collectors are thrilled. Others find selling a pet's ashes a bit much. Some say important items should go to libraries or museums, not private buyers.
stories.image_alt: Truman Capote at home among his belongings

terms.explain: A sale where people bid, and the highest offer wins.
Everything a person owned when they died.
Someone who writes the story of another person's life.

stories.headline: At least 39 people die after a migrant boat sinks off Senegal on the way to Spain's Canary Islands
stories.dek: Only one survivor found so far; the Atlantic route is one of the deadliest in the world.
stories.caveman: Many young people in West Africa try to reach Europe by taking small wooden boats across the Atlantic to Spain's Canary Islands. A boat sank between Dakar, Senegal's capital, and the northern city of Saint-Louis. At least 39 people died and one was rescued; it is not known how many are missing. Rescuers are searching 25km of coast, but strong currents push bodies away. Senegal's president urged young people not to risk the trip and promised to fight the smugglers. A Spanish rights group counted 635 deaths on this route in just January to May 2026, and estimates about 21 people die for every 100 who arrive.
stories.why_it_matters: People take this risk because they see no future at home — no jobs, climate damage, and depleted fishing. It is a global story about poverty and borders.
stories.camps: Governments focus on stopping smugglers and patrolling seas. Rights groups say safe, legal ways to migrate would save lives. Some in Europe want tougher borders; others say Europe's fishing fleets and trade policies helped cause the problem.
stories.image_alt: A migrant boat on the Atlantic route to the Canary Islands (file photo)

terms.explain: A person who moves to another country, often to find work or safety.
People paid to move others across borders illegally.
Spanish islands off the coast of West Africa — the closest part of Europe.

stories.headline: Comedian Russell Brand is sentenced to 10½ years in prison for rape and sexual assault
stories.dek: Six women testified; four gave statements in court. He denies the charges.
stories.caveman: Russell Brand is a British comedian and actor who was very famous in the 2000s, later became a conspiracy-theory influencer popular with the US right. A London jury found him guilty of raping a woman in 2009 and sexually assaulting three women between 2004 and 2009. On Monday the judge sentenced him to 10 years and 6 months. Six women testified over four weeks; none were named publicly. Four told the court how the attacks changed their lives — one spoke from behind a curtain. Critics say his mistreatment of women was an "open secret" in entertainment for years. Brand denies all charges. Separately, his ex-partner Jemima Goldsmith said he physically assaulted her.
stories.why_it_matters: The case shows that powerful, famous men can be held to account, even decades later. It also raises questions about who in the industry knew and stayed silent.
stories.camps: Women's-rights groups call it a win for survivors who were not believed for years. Brand's supporters claim he is being targeted for his views. Legal experts note the jury cleared him of three of seven counts — the process weighed each charge.
stories.image_alt: Court sketch of Russell Brand in the dock at Southwark Crown Court
stories.image_credit: Photo: Elizabeth Cook / PA via AP, NPR

terms.explain: When a judge decides the punishment after a guilty verdict.
Words from victims telling the court how a crime hurt them.
Something many people know but don't say publicly.
Ordinary citizens chosen to decide guilt in a trial.

stories.headline: In Gaza, a rain-soaked sand bank collapses on tents of displaced families, killing five including two children
stories.dek: UN says 26,000+ households had shelters damaged in weekend storms.
stories.caveman: Most of Gaza's people have lost their homes in the war and now live in tents. Heavy rain and wind hit over the weekend. On Sunday near Deir al-Balah, a sand bank above a camp collapsed and buried at least three tents. Five people died, including a mother and her children aged eight and six. The father survived because he was outside — one child had just called him to come and eat. Neighbors dug with hammers, shovels and flashlights and had to break a huge boulder to reach people. The UN says more than 26,000 households reported damage to tents or belongings after the storms.
stories.why_it_matters: Winter is just starting. Without real homes, warm clothes and safe camp sites, more people — especially children — are in danger.
stories.camps: Aid groups say Israel must let in more shelter materials and supplies. Israel says it allows aid and blames Hamas. Many people simply want both sides to put civilians' safety first.
stories.image_alt: Aftermath of the embankment collapse in Deir al-Balah
stories.image_credit: Photo: Ahmed Ibrahim / APAImages / Shutterstock via The Guardian

terms.explain: Forced to leave home, often living in camps or tents.
When earth, sand or rocks suddenly slide down a slope.
Food, water, shelter and medicine for people in crisis.

stories.headline: 'Settle down or we'll arrest you': Australian report finds Queensland police push rape cases to the back of the line
stories.dek: About two-thirds of sexual-assault reports end withdrawn, unproven or unsolved; overworked detectives say serious cases sit for a year.
stories.caveman: A new study by the Australian Institute of Criminology looked at why so many sexual-assault complaints in Queensland, Australia, go nowhere — about two-thirds. Detectives said they are overloaded and pushed to focus on "political" crimes like youth theft, so rape cases go "on the backburner," sometimes for 12 months. Victims were interviewed in shared offices or a changing room. Some were told to "settle down" or face arrest. Getting a forensic rape exam could mean driving up to seven hours. Cases handled by specially trained sex-crime officers were much less likely to drop out.
stories.why_it_matters: When reporting rape feels hopeless, fewer survivors come forward and attackers face no consequences. The fixes — trained officers, private rooms, exam access — apply in many countries, including Taiwan.
stories.camps: Survivor advocates say the report proves what victims have said for years. Police unions say officers are stretched too thin and need more staff. Researchers say the evidence favors specialist teams.
stories.image_alt: Illustration for report on police handling of sexual assault cases in Queensland

terms.explain: A person who experienced a crime like sexual assault — a word that respects their strength.
Here: cases that drop out before reaching court.
A medical check that collects evidence after an assault.
Treating people in a way that understands how trauma affects them.
